en: That is my counsel; understand it.
Oh, heroic Kiyaz, heed my words.
You were a heedless khan,
Great in courage but without sense,
A rash and simple soul.
I drew upon the learned elders;
I asked the knowledgeable.
My account may be incomplete:
Within Aychörök
There is, perhaps four or five months along,
A child left by the mighty warrior.
When Chörök goes into labor,
Against that fierce black troublemaker,
Gather in full ninety witches
And forty old women.
Find one who knows incantations,
An infidel who knows sorcery,
And have them sow trouble beforehand.
When Chörök gives birth,
Make her drink a potion and grow drunk,
Then steal away her child.
Let not a single soul know;
Let not a single person see.
Before anyone can utter a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Steal away the child
Of that raging Chörök.
To a dungeon forty rope-lengths deep,
If her child is a boy,
Find a way to steal him away,
And put an end to him.
If it is not a boy but a girl,
Say, “My wife has borne a child”;
Slaughter ninety sheep for her feast,
And give her whatever name you choose.
Part and comb the hair at her temples,
And saying, “This has turned out well,”
Give her away where she will not weep.
But if the child is a boy,
He will not let you turn your plow.
If by chance you leave him alive,
If by chance he survives,
Then the Jediger of Jeti-Özön—
You are finished, valiant Kiyaz;
You will be slaughtered and eat filth.
When he reaches twelve,
He will roam your hills and raise dust;
He will lay low anyone he grapples.
His pounding tread will raise dust,
And bring renown to your mighty people.
Do not boast of strength, Kiyaz:
If you wrestle him, he will bloody your head!
He will dig your grave layer by layer
And make your misery boil;
Before your very eyes he will show you
A marvel no man has ever wrought.
He will take a spear and fight the host,
Demanding, “Find my father for me!”
He will quarrel not only with you, Kiyaz,
But with the whole face of the earth.
If it happens that you come to blows,
If by chance she bears a son,
He will dig your deep grave;
If you swarm him, he will slaughter your host.
Before your very eyes he will show you
A wonder dreadful for man to behold.
That is my counsel; understand it.
Be wary, Kiyaz, and heed my words!
All his earliest forefathers were khans,
Blessed by Kydyr from their very roots;
All his chief ancestors were khans.
He is the offspring of calamity,
Blessed by Kydyr from the beginning.
His forefather through his father—
The son who remains after him—
Will grow to manhood as an orphan
And somehow take his place among the people.
Just look at his maturity:
When he reaches twelve,
He will break a fortress and take plunder,
And embroil mighty peoples in strife.
Just look at his devastation!
When he reaches thirteen,
He will draw Zulpukor and wield it;
The sullen foe will vanish,
And he will rise boldly and prevail.
Before the offspring of this troublemaker,
Every man who faces him will vanish.
He will spare no hero;
No opponent will remain.
The offspring of such an infidel—
His lashes are flame and his eyes are embers;
Among men there is no such scourge.
His brow is high and his gaze direct;
Provoke him, and his harsh words strike true.
A gray tiger will walk before him;
In all the world there will be no such hero.
He is the son of suspect kin—
Know that the child will be an enemy;
If the child lives and grows,
He will come after all of us
And become our greatest foe.
Wise Kiyaz, heed my words:
Though his outward form is different,
At heart he will bear us enmity;
That child is not one of our people at root.
When the child is born,
If by chance it is a son,
Be sure to post guards outside!
Find a way to steal him,
And devise the means with care.
My husband Kiyaz, think;
I tell you often—please heed my words.
Put aside your worry until the birth.
If this Chörök bears a son,
Find a way to dispose of her child.
That is how matters stand with the child;
Heroic Kiyaz, listen,
And know that I have warned you hoarse!
Ah, my dear Kiyaz, heed my words:
If it is a girl, leave her alive;
But if the child is a boy,
Find the means somehow to slaughter him.
They spoke weighty, masterful words,
Making their pledge firm,
Swearing an oath binding unto death:
May whoever breaks it die.
They caught upon the hillside
A gray mare like a white pavilion,
Held that mare for the oath,
And slaughtered it before the people.
As black blood flowed from the mare,
They cupped it in both hands and smeared themselves.
They made a solemn covenant,
Saying, “Let this befall whoever holds back.”
They licked the edge of white steel
And chewed grains of white wheat.
Kanchoro and valiant Kiyaz
Clasped hands as heroes,
Saying that whoever failed to do this
Was an infidel for seven generations.
Speaking quietly and resolving firmly,
Heroic Kiyaz began:
“You have been my friend, my Kanchoro.
As for the child in her womb,
I shall whip him and take his head;
When the child is born,
I shall put an end to him!
My wise khan, my Kanchoro,
I shall heed your words.
Sixty plots and eighty schemes,
Foul designs and twisted designs—
I shall ponder them all.
When her child is born,
I shall slaughter him while still an infant.
While the child is still in the caul,
If it is not female but male,
I shall put an end to him.
You spoke, my khan, and I listened.
You yourself spoke of what comes first,
My wise one, my Kanchoro,
And you yourself foresaw what follows.
My hero and kinsman on every side,
The affliction of these six years—
You who can now perceive it,
My open-eyed hero,
My watchful Kanchoro,
You are my black ridge hung with protection,
My lion-hearted kinsman!
You rekindle the extinguished fire
And bring the dead soul back to life;
My hero, fertile in wisdom,
My resourceful champion.”
So valiant Kiyaz spoke
And swore his oath to Kanchoro;
He carried the oath through to its end.
Then Kanchoro grew wrathful.
Once the matter had gone thus,
Once the words had found their place,
Once the speech had gone thus,
Once the speech had settled in its place,
The people rose clamoring, “We agree!”
When all the great black host of Jediger
Stood behind him without exception,
When the words Choro had spoken
Won the assent of all the people—
God forbid that one should see his face!
Such was Kanchoro's bearing:
Blood suffused his noble eyes,
Fire swept across his blood-red face.
He donned an arrow-proof coat
And mounted a horse no arrow could reach.
He took the pale banner in hand.
If you had seen Choro's form,
He stood built like a lofty mountain.
Choro's two cheeks looked
As though two Dangyt men had eaten their fill.
If anyone challenged Kanchoro,
He looked ready to slaughter the challenger;
If his wrath fell upon the Kyrgyz,
He looked able simply to wipe them out.
At that time Kanchoro
Wore a black cap broad as a cauldron.
He had the will to slaughter
Not only the Kyrgyz but the whole world.
If Choro surged forward,
No mountain could withstand him;
Even the Kyrgyz in all their multitude
Could not defeat this Choro.
He sprang like a tiger;
No one who fought him would survive.
He made ready like a wild boar.
The great host was struck speechless
And simply despaired of life;
Unable to collect their wits,
The people clamored in bewilderment.
A calamity befell the multitude:
Fierce as a mountain, potent in venom,
Choro stood roaring.
Without speaking or saying a word,
The great people stood crushed.
He spoke like a storm and began his address,
Overwhelming the assembled people.
Jylgyn and Keng-Kol became a ravine;
Kanchoro arose from among his own
To become, for the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
An enemy worse than the Chinese.
The dear people sobbed and wept,
Grieving in utter anguish,
Bereft of their mighty warrior.
“What kind of age is this?” they cried,
And all the people stood lamenting.
At the wrath of Khan Kanchoro,
Khan and commoner alike were amazed.
Kanchoro began his fury;
The people who witnessed it
Renounced not only their livestock
But even life itself.
He donned his arrow-proof coat,
As though about to plunge deep into battle.
He split the tail of his mount
Diagonally and tied it in a hard knot.
He turned his tulpar's head;
The crested banner appeared in his hand.
The hearts of all the watching people
Were torn grievously apart.
The Grey Wolf's hardy sons cried,
“What age is this, what day?
What sort of night must we behold?”
The people clamored and grieved;
The birch wept and the willow wept,
Every living soul who looked on wept,
The men who claimed courage wept;
Look—the black earth itself wept.
The dear Argyn and Kyrgyz people
Moved among them, wailing.
